Debounce waits for the burst to end and runs only the last call; a leading-edge throttle runs the first call and silently drops everything after it, including the last one.

### Debounce
- Keep one `Timer?`. Every call cancels the pending timer and starts a new one, so the action runs only after `delay` of silence.
- The action closes over the latest arguments, so the request carries the final text, not the first.
- 300 ms is the working value for search: shorter and you pay for keystrokes, longer and the field feels stuck.

### Throttle
- Leading edge: run now, record the time, ignore calls until the window passes. That is what you want for scroll and drag handlers.
- Trailing edge: remember the last arguments and fire once at the end of the window — the shape for autosave-while-typing.
- Throttling a search field is the classic wrong choice: `flu` goes to the network and `flutter` is discarded, so the user sees results for a prefix they already finished typing.

### The trap
- The `Timer` outlives the widget. Cancel it in `dispose`, or the callback fires on a disposed `State` and you get "setState() called after dispose()".
- Constructing the `Debouncer` inside `build` gives every rebuild its own timer, which debounces nothing. It belongs on the `State` (or a controller) as a field.

Rule of thumb: debounce means "wait until they stop typing", throttle means "at most once per window". Text input debounces; scroll, drag and analytics pings throttle.

Fold the flat list into a `Map<DateTime, List<Txn>>` keyed by the date with the time stripped, then sort the keys — the grouping is one pass and about five lines.

### The fold
- The accumulator is the map; for each item compute the key, `putIfAbsent(key, () => [])` and add. `putIfAbsent` runs the factory only on a miss, so there is one lookup path and no `containsKey` dance.
- `groupBy` from `package:collection` is exactly this with a name. Use it in production; write the fold once in the interview to show the mechanism is not magic.
- A plain `for` wins the moment you accumulate more than one thing — nobody enjoys reading a fold whose accumulator is a record of three buckets.

### Why the key betrays you
- `DateTime` equality is exact to the microsecond and also compares the `isUtc` flag, so two timestamps from the same day never collide. Truncate with `DateTime(d.year, d.month, d.day)`.
- Group in the user's zone. Server timestamps are UTC, and a purchase at 01:30 local is yesterday in UTC — call `toLocal()` before truncating or half your users see the wrong header.

### Order
- A Dart map literal is a `LinkedHashMap`, so keys come out in insertion order — the API's order, which is not necessarily newest-first. Sort the key list explicitly.
- `ListView.builder` wants an indexable list, not a map: flatten the sections into a `List<Row>` of headers and items once, in the state, never inside `build`.

A `sealed class Result<T, E>` with `Ok` and `Err` subtypes moves failure into the return type, so the compiler — not code review — is what forces every caller to deal with it.

### The type
- `sealed` closes the hierarchy, so a `switch` over a `Result` is exhaustive at compile time. Mark `Ok` and `Err` `final` so nobody adds a third arm from another library.
- Two type parameters, not one: `E` typed as `Object` is try/catch with extra syntax. Make `E` a sealed error enum of its own so the UI can switch on it.
- `map` transforms the value and passes `Err` through untouched, `mapError` is the mirror, and `fold` collapses both arms into one value — usually a widget or a message.
- `flatMap` is the one people forget: `map` with a function that itself returns a `Result` gives you `Result<Result<...>>`.

### At the call site
- One try/catch, at the boundary that actually knows the failure modes — the repository. Above it nothing catches anything, and there is no exception to forget.
- The call site reads as a pipeline: `map` to reshape, `flatMap` to chain another fallible step, `fold` to land on a widget.

### Where it stops paying
- `map` does not catch. If the function you pass throws, the exception escapes the `Result` and you are back where you started; a fallible step belongs in `flatMap`.
- Programming errors — a bad index, a null assertion, a broken invariant — should crash, not become an `Err` you render as a snackbar. Wrap I/O, not bugs.
- Dart has no `?` propagation operator, so long chains get noisy. That is the price; `fold` at the end is what keeps it readable.

Walk both lists with two indices, always taking the smaller head, and keep a `Set<String>` of ids already emitted: O(n + m) time, one pass, no second sort.

### The merge
- Two cursors. Compare the heads with `compareTo`, append the smaller, advance that cursor; when one list runs out, drain the other.
- Concatenating and sorting is O((n + m) log(n + m)) and throws away the one fact you were given — that both inputs are already ordered. Saying that out loud is the point of the question.
- Ties need a written-down rule. Equal timestamps are common (bulk inserts, second-resolution servers), so break them on `id` or the order changes between runs and the list visibly jitters.

### Dedupe
- `Set.add` returns `false` when the element was already there, so the membership test and the insert are one call and one hash lookup.
- `out.any((m) => m.id == id)` is the version that makes the whole merge quadratic — the classic way to lose an otherwise correct answer.
- Decide which copy survives. The server's is usually newer, so on an id collision take the fresh one and skip the cached one. If the server can also change the timestamp of an existing id, the id set is not enough: index the fresh page by id and prefer it explicitly.

### The DateTime trap
- `a.sentAt == b.sentAt` is `false` for the same instant when one side is UTC and the other local — `DateTime`'s `==` compares the `isUtc` flag too.
- Compare with `compareTo` or `isAtSameMomentAs`, which look only at the instant, and store one zone (UTC) end to end.

Pre-order DFS with an explicit stack: push the roots reversed, then pop a node, emit `(comment, depth)`, and push its children reversed so they come back out in reading order.

### Why a stack and not recursion
- A stack reverses whatever you push, so pushing children left to right makes them pop right to left. Push `children.reversed` — that one detail is what the exercise is testing.
- Recursion is fine at depth five and dies on a pathological reply chain. Dart's stack overflow is not something you can catch and recover from, and comment depth is user-controlled input.
- Depth belongs on the stack entry, not on the model. The same comment sits at depth 0 in a permalink view and depth 7 in the thread.

### What it buys the UI
- `ListView.builder` needs a count and an index; a tree offers neither, so it would build every node eagerly. Flatten once per data change, keep the result in state, and the list virtualizes again.
- Collapsing a subtree becomes one `if`: skip pushing the children of a collapsed node. Nothing else in the walk changes.
- Cap the visual indent — `min(depth, 6) * 12` — or a deep thread renders as a diagonal sliver of text.

### If the API sends a flat list with parentId
- Build a `Map<String?, List<Comment>>` of children first with `groupBy`, then run the same walk over it.
- Searching the flat list for each node's children inside the loop is the O(n²) version that looks innocent and dies at a thousand comments.

Wrap the function in a closure over a `Map` and use a Dart record `(a, b)` as the key — a `List` key never hits, because `List` equality is identity.

### The key
- A `Map` finds entries by `==` and `hashCode`. `['eu', 2.0] == ['eu', 2.0]` is `false`, so every call misses, the map grows forever, and the "cache" is pure overhead.
- A record `(String, double)` has structural equality and a matching `hashCode` generated by the language, so a later call with equal arguments finds the entry. Since Dart 3 that is the whole answer.
- The pre-records habit was `'$a|$b'`, which breaks as soon as an argument can contain the separator — `('a|b', 'c')` and `('a', 'b|c')` produce the same string.
- A small class with `==`/`hashCode` (or Equatable) does the same job when the key deserves a name.

### Storing an absent value
- `cache[key] ??= compute(key)` recomputes forever if the function can legitimately return `null`, because a stored `null` is indistinguishable from a miss.
- `putIfAbsent` calls the factory exactly once per missing key and stores whatever it returns, `null` included. Prefer it, or check `containsKey`.

### What memoization requires
- Purity. Memoizing something that reads `DateTime.now()`, a locale or a feature flag freezes the first answer — put that input in the key, or do not memoize.
- A bound. An unbounded map on a repository that outlives the screen is a leak: cap it with an LRU, or clear it when the inputs change.
- A real cost. A map lookup plus a record allocation is not free; memoizing a 2 µs function makes it slower.

A Dart `Map` is a `LinkedHashMap` that preserves insertion order, so an LRU is that map plus two moves: on a hit remove the key and re-insert it, and on an insert past capacity remove `keys.first`.

### The implementation
- `get`: `remove(key)`, then write it back. That re-insertion is what makes the entry most-recent. Reading `map[key]` alone leaves the order untouched and your LRU is quietly a FIFO — the bug the interviewer is waiting for.
- `put`: `remove` first so an existing key moves to the end, write the value, then evict while `length > capacity`. Only a new key can push you over; updating an existing one must never evict.
- The textbook answer is "hash map plus a doubly linked list". `LinkedHashMap` is exactly that, already written: it hashes to the entry and unlinks it from the entry list.

### Costs
- `get` O(1), `put` O(1) amortized, eviction O(1) per entry, memory O(capacity).
- `keys.first` reads the head of the entry list — it does not scan, so eviction stays constant.
- Never `remove` while iterating `keys`; take the key into a local first or you get a `ConcurrentModificationError`.

### In a real app
- A nullable `V` breaks the `remove`-returns-null shortcut, because a stored `null` looks like a miss. Guard with `containsKey` when `V` can be null.
- Bound by cost, not by count, when entries differ wildly in size. Decoded images want a byte budget — Flutter's own `ImageCache` exposes `maximumSize` and `maximumSizeBytes` for that reason.
- LRU keeps whatever the user just touched, which is the wrong policy for freshness. A feed wants a TTL; a thumbnail cache wants LRU.

Keep a `Map<String, Future<T>>` of the requests currently in flight and hand every later caller the same `Future` — a Dart `Future` is a value you can await any number of times, and the work behind it runs once.

### The helper
- Look the key up; on a hit return the running future, on a miss start the call and store it. `putIfAbsent` expresses that in one line.
- The key must contain everything that identifies the request — path plus every parameter — or two different profiles share one answer.
- Remove the entry in `whenComplete`, which runs on both the value and the error path. Now the map holds only work that is actually in flight: this is de-duplication, not caching, and the next call after completion really does go to the network.

### The trap
- Leaving the future in the map turns it into a cache you never designed. One 500 is then replayed to every caller forever, and a success goes stale with nothing to invalidate it. `then` alone leaks exactly the failure case.
- A future that completes with an error and has no listener becomes an unhandled async error. Here the first caller always awaits, so it is fine — it breaks if you "warm" the map with a future nobody awaits.
- Nothing gets cancelled. If the first caller navigates away the request still finishes, and the others still get their answer, which is usually what you want; if it is not, you need a `CancelToken` and a refcount.

### Where it belongs
- In the repository, not the widget. Providers, `FutureBuilder`s and initState calls all funnel through it, and mounting a screen costs one request.
- The same shape fixes the token-refresh stampede: five parallel 401s must trigger one refresh, keyed on a single constant string.

Order is the free half — `Future.wait` returns results in argument order no matter who finishes first; the work is bounding how many run at once, and that needs a pool fed with functions, not with futures that have already started.

### Why the obvious line fails
- `Future.wait(ids.map(api.fetch))` starts all 50 the moment `map` is iterated. A `Future` is work already in progress, not a description of work, so anything that means to schedule it must take `Future<T> Function()` thunks.
- Chunking with `slices(4)` from `package:collection` does bound it, but one slow item idles three workers until the whole chunk finishes, so utilisation collapses on a long tail.

### The worker pool
- Pre-size `List<R?>.filled(n, null)`, keep one shared cursor, and run `limit` worker loops that each take the next index and write into that slot. Order comes from the slot, never from completion time.
- Reading the cursor and bumping it with no `await` in between is what makes it race-free: the isolate is single-threaded, so only an `await` can interleave two workers.
- `Pool(4).withResource(() => api.fetch(id))` from `package:pool` is the same thing off the shelf, and it composes with `Future.wait`.

### Errors
- One thrown future completes `Future.wait` with that error while the other 49 keep running unobserved; their later failures surface as uncaught errors in the zone.
- Decide explicitly: `eagerError: true` to fail fast, or a try/catch around each task storing a `Result` per slot, so one 500 does not throw away 49 good responses.

Rule of thumb: bound with a pool, order with an index, and never create a `Future` before you are ready for it to run.

Type the bus by event class and hand the caller back a `StreamSubscription` it has to cancel — a bus keyed by strings that stores `void Function(Object)` callbacks has no way of knowing a screen is gone.

### The shape
- One `StreamController<Object>.broadcast()`, and `on<T>()` returns `_ctrl.stream.where((e) => e is T).cast<T>()`. `dart:async` has no `whereType` on `Stream`; that operator is rxdart's.
- Events are classes, so a typo is a compile error and the payload is typed. String keys give you neither.
- A broadcast controller buffers nothing: an event fired with no listener is gone, and a screen that subscribes later has missed it. If the newcomer needs the current value, that is a `ValueNotifier` or rxdart's `BehaviorSubject`, not a bus.

### How the listener outlives the screen
- The callback closes over `this`, so it pins the `State`, its `Element` and the whole subtree that element built. The bus is normally a singleton, so that graph lives until the process dies.
- Broadcast subscriptions are never cancelled for you. A missed `cancel()` is not a crash, it is silent memory growth plus a duplicated side effect every time the screen is re-entered — and then `setState` after `dispose` throws somewhere unrelated.

### Making the leak structurally impossible
- Return `Stream<T>` from the bus and let `StreamBuilder` own the subscription: it cancels in its own `dispose`, so there is nothing left to forget.
- When you must `listen` yourself, collect the subscriptions in a list and cancel them all in `dispose`, and switch on the `cancel_subscriptions` and `close_sinks` lints so the analyser finds the field you forgot.

A bus that only exposes streams cannot leak more than its listener does; a bus that stores callbacks in a map has to be trusted, and trust is the part that leaks.

The four fields are the easy part; the bug is that page three's response can land after the refresh has already reset the list, so the controller needs a generation counter that turns every in-flight response into a no-op.

### The state
- `items`, `cursor`, `hasMore`, `loading`, `error`. A null `cursor` means "from the start", which is exactly the state `refresh()` restores.
- `hasMore` comes from the server returning a null next cursor, not from `page.length < pageSize`. A backend that filters after paging legitimately returns a short page that is not the last one.

### The guard
- Bail out on `loading`, on `!hasMore`, and on a non-null `error`. Dropping that third condition is the classic bug: the scroll trigger fires every pixel, so a failing endpoint gets re-hit once per frame.
- A failure must not advance the cursor. Keep the cursor you sent, surface the error, and let `retry()` be nothing more than "clear the error and call `loadMore` again" — the identical request goes back out.

### The refresh race
- `refresh()` bumps `_generation` before it starts. Every `await` in `loadMore` is followed by `if (gen != _generation) return;`, so a stale page can append neither its items nor its cursor.
- The same counter covers a changed search query, which is this race wearing a different hat.
- `copyWith` cannot put a nullable field back to null, so clearing `error` means constructing the state directly or passing a sentinel.

Test it with a fake repository that hands out a `Completer` per page: you can then assert that a second `loadMore()` during flight does nothing, and that a response completed after `refresh()` changes no state at all.

Keep a queue of the timestamps you have already granted: a call is admitted immediately while fewer than N of them fall inside the window, otherwise it is scheduled for the moment the oldest one ages out.

### Rolling window, not a resetting counter
- A counter cleared every minute lets 2N through in two seconds across the boundary — five at 11:59:59 and five at 12:00:01. The queue of stamps is what makes the window roll.
- Memory is O(N), not O(calls): you prune everything older than the window on each admission, so the queue never exceeds N plus the slots you have booked ahead.
- A token bucket is the other correct answer — refill N per window, capacity N, O(1) state — and it is what most servers actually run. Say which one you are building and why.

### Keeping it race-free
- Compute the grant time and push it onto the queue with no `await` between those two steps, then wait. If you wait first and record afterwards, two concurrent callers both see room and both go.
- Because the reservation is for a future instant, callers stack up in arrival order instead of all waking at once when the window slides.

### Testing without sleeping
- Take the clock from a seam: `clock.now()` from `package:clock` instead of `DateTime.now()`, and `Future.delayed` for the wait.
- `fakeAsync` from `package:fake_async` — the same one `flutter_test` uses — replaces the zone's timers *and* installs a `Clock` that moves with them, so `async.elapse(const Duration(minutes: 1))` advances both in microseconds.
- Assert on the decision, not on wall time: five of six calls complete at elapsed zero, the sixth at exactly one minute.

Anything that reads `DateTime.now()` or sleeps directly is untestable by construction. Inject both seams and the suite checks an hour of behaviour in a millisecond.

An `Iterable` is a factory for `Iterator`s: you implement `get iterator`, and the whole contract is that every call returns a *fresh* iterator positioned before the first element.

### The iterator contract
- `moveNext()` advances and returns false at the end; `current` is only defined after `moveNext()` returned true, which is why a null-safe `E current` usually has a `late` field behind it.
- Extend `IterableBase<E>` from `dart:collection` and you get `map`, `where`, `length`, `toList` and the rest for free, all driven by your `moveNext`. Implementing the `Iterable` interface directly means writing dozens of methods by hand.
- Returning the same iterator instance twice is the classic bug: the second `for-in` finds it exhausted and silently sees nothing.

### What laziness buys and costs
- Nothing runs until someone iterates, so `windows(list, 2).first` builds exactly one window. Iterating twice re-runs everything — cheap over a list, a second network call over anything else.
- The SDK's own collections throw `ConcurrentModificationError` when the backing list changes mid-iteration, because they carry a modification count. A hand-rolled iterator has no such check unless you add one, and returns quietly wrong results instead.

### Why sync* is usually the answer
- `sync*` compiles into exactly that state machine: locals become the iterator's fields and each `yield` is a suspension point resumed by `moveNext()`. Thirty lines become three, with identical laziness.
- `yield*` delegates into another iterable, so a lazy pre-order tree walk is a two-line function.
- Hand-roll only for what a generator cannot give you: an iterator someone else drives (a parser, a k-way merge), an O(1) `length` or `contains` override, or resettable state you want to expose.

Build it as a `StreamTransformer.fromBind` over an `async*` function, so the filter state — the last fix you kept — is created fresh on every `bind`, and gate on the fix's own timestamp rather than on the device clock.

### The two gates
- Both compare against the last **emitted** fix, not the last received one. Comparing against the previous input turns a slow walk into a stream that drops everything and never emits again.
- Check time before distance: a subtraction is free, the haversine is four trig calls. The first fix always passes both.
- `Geolocator.distanceBetween(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2)` already returns metres if `geolocator` is in the project; hand-roll the haversine only when the interviewer asks you to.

### Why fromBind and not fromHandlers
- `StreamTransformer.fromHandlers` stores the `handleData` closure once, so whatever state that closure captures is shared by every stream the transformer is bound to. Reuse one instance across two subscriptions and their filters corrupt each other.
- `fromBind` calls your function per `bind`, and an `async*` body allocates fresh locals each time. It also gives you backpressure for free: `await for` pauses the source while the listener is paused.
- The result is single-subscription. If the source was broadcast and several widgets listen, add `.asBroadcastStream()` after the transform or you get "Stream has already been listened to".

### Run on the data's clock
- Fixes arrive in a burst after a tunnel or a wake-up. Throttling on `DateTime.now()` keeps whichever fix happened to arrive first; throttling on `fix.timestamp` keeps the right one and makes the transformer testable with a plain list of fabricated fixes.

Rule of thumb: throttle on the event's own clock, and always compare against what you last let through.

Walk both structures together carrying a path, and return the first mismatch as a string like `$.user.tags[1]` instead of a bool — a plain `==` on two maps compares identity, which is the only reason this function has to exist at all.

### What the SDK gives you
- `Map` and `List` inherit `==` from `Object`, so two structurally identical payloads are unequal. Two identical `const` literals *are* equal, because const values are canonicalised — which is what makes the bug so confusing in tests.
- `package:collection` has `DeepCollectionEquality().equals(a, b)` with a matching `hash`, plus `.unordered()` for when list order carries no meaning. It answers "are they equal" correctly and never answers "where", which is the whole point of the exercise.

### The walk
- Recurse into `Map` and `List`, compare everything else with `==`. Report in a fixed order: type mismatch, key present on one side only, length mismatch, then leaf inequality.
- Sort the union of the keys before iterating. Dart maps iterate in insertion order, so two payloads assembled in different orders would otherwise report different "first" differences.
- Cap the depth, or track visited objects, if the input can contain a cycle. Decoded JSON cannot; a graph of domain objects can, and unguarded recursion becomes a stack overflow.

### Leaves that lie
- `double.nan != double.nan`, so a payload containing NaN is not equal to itself. Special-case it or the diff blames a field nobody touched.
- `1 == 1.0` is true, but `jsonDecode` returns `int` for `1` and `double` for `1.0`, so a strict `runtimeType` check flags a difference the API does not have. Compare `num`s by value, everything else by type as well.

Return `null` for "equal" and write `expect(firstDiff(expected, actual), isNull)` — the failure message is then the path itself.

A trie makes the prefix lookup O(len(prefix)) plus the cost of collecting matches, but for 50 000 short names a sorted list with two binary searches beats it on memory and on build time — the trie earns its place when you need payloads in the nodes, ranked completions or fuzzy walks.

### Building it
- A node is a map from code unit to child, plus the ids that end there. Insert is `putIfAbsent(c, TrieNode.new)` per character, so building the whole index is O(total characters).
- Lookup walks the prefix, then does a DFS under that node — **cap the DFS**. A one-letter query sits above tens of thousands of words, and the naive collector walks all of them before the user types the second letter.
- Index a normalised key (lowercased, diacritics folded) and keep the display string as the payload, or "Café" never matches "cafe".

### The numbers that decide it
- 50 000 names of ~20 characters share prefixes down to roughly 300 000 nodes. Each node is a Dart object owning a `Map`, on the order of 150 bytes once the map's own storage counts — tens of megabytes, which on a phone is the whole argument against it.
- The sorted `List<String>` is the same 50 000 strings, a couple of megabytes, and a prefix search is `lowerBound(q)` to `lowerBound(bump(q))`: about sixteen comparisons and one contiguous slice.
- A linear `where((n) => n.startsWith(q))` over 50 000 costs a millisecond or two on a mid-range phone. That fits in a frame, so for one keystroke it is genuinely fine; it stops being fine when it runs per keystroke on the UI isolate while the list is scrolling.

### When neither is the answer
- Infix matching — "case" finding "Phone case" — defeats a prefix trie and a sorted list alike. That is an inverted index over tokens, or FTS5 through `sqflite`, which is what ships in most offline search features.

Measure first: the scan until it shows up in a profile, the sorted index when it does, the trie when the query is more than a prefix.
